source: Na, Grossmann, Varnum, Kitayama, Gonzalez & Nisbett (2010) Cultural differences are not always reducible to individual differences. PNAS 107(14):6192-6197 (full text, PMC)
finding: Founding study read in full. One US sample of 235 adults from a phone directory, ages 25-93, tested on 10 social-orientation and 10 cognitive-style measures over three sessions. Correlations among measures inside the sample are near zero.
numbers: N=235 (all Americans, diverse social class). Social orientation: mean r=.008, median r=.008 over 45 pairs; only 2 of 45 significant and positive; first factor 12.26% of variance (chance level for 10 measures is 10%). Cognitive style: mean r=.038, median .040; first factor 10.69%. For contrast: WAIS-IV subtests mean r=.48; NEO-PI-R facet loadings mean .64.
quote: the correlations among the measures were negligible
limits: Only one country. Social-class contrast is the only group split inside the sample. Per-pair table is in the SI (not read).
agent_relevance: Closes gap 1 for the primary numbers. A style label from one task does not predict style on another task for one person.

source: Na et al. (2010) PNAS, group-level validity section
finding: The same measures do separate groups: working class vs middle class. This is the core 'group yes, individual no' contrast.
numbers: Social orientation: working class more interdependent on 7 of 10 measures, 4 significant, 1 opposite; aggregate t(188)=2.81, p<.01. Cognitive style: working class more holistic on 7 of 10, 5 significant (one marginal), 1 opposite; aggregate t(213)=3.51, p<.001. Published East Asian vs Western effect sizes used to pick measures: mean d=.54 (social), d=.62 (cognitive).
limits: Class difference tested in one US sample. The aggregate index is built from the same weak measures.
agent_relevance: An aggregate can sort groups even when single tasks do not agree for individuals. Do not read a person's style from one probe.

source: Na et al. (2010) PNAS, five-culture check of two tasks
finding: Two tasks (framed line task and attribution) from five cultures show a strong culture-level link and almost none at the person level.
numbers: Cultures: US, UK, Germany, Croatia, Japan. Individual-level r=.04 with all pooled; median within-culture r=-.047; US plus Japan only r=.070. Culture-level r=.73. Multilevel second-level random-effect correlation .82.
limits: Only two tasks, a secondary analysis; sample sizes per culture not given in the main text.
agent_relevance: Best single illustration of the ecological-fallacy risk: culture r=.73 versus person r about 0.

source: Na et al. (2010) PNAS, simulation and reliability argument
finding: The authors show with algebra and simulation that zero within-group correlation plus a group effect gives only a tiny pooled correlation, so near-zero person-level links are expected. They also argue reliability does not explain the result.
numbers: Two variables with group d=.4 pooled give r about .039 (limit .038). Simulation: 2 groups of n=100, 10 variables, d=.4, within-group r=0; mean pooled r=.038 over 10,000 runs. d=1 gives r about .2. Test-retest of one measure (exclusion task), 1-4 weeks apart: r=.51. Excluding measures with alpha<.60: mean r=.031, median .072.
limits: Reliability table (Table S3) not read. Test-retest given for one measure only. Authors' own interpretation; a low-reliability reading is not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 7: modest reliability (test-retest .51 for one task) caps possible correlations but does not make them near zero.

source: Na et al. (2010) PNAS, interpretation and prior small studies
finding: Authors cite earlier small studies (Caudill & Schooler on Japanese vs American children; Kitayama and colleagues on Japanese and US students) with the same pattern, and offer a post-hoc reason: groups socialise members toward shared self-definition, but do not press the same degree on each sub-component.
numbers: No new numbers; the earlier studies used few measures and restricted samples, which the authors call inconclusive.
limits: Explanation is untested. The paper itself says stable individual profiles per measure may exist (test-retest .51).
agent_relevance: Two earlier small studies agree, but they are from the authors' circle; no independent large replication was found.

source: Lu, Song & Zhang (2025) Cultural tendencies in generative AI. Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Abstract read (rest paywalled). GPT answers more interdependent and more holistic in Chinese than English; ERNIE replicates; GPT recommends more interdependent ads in Chinese; exploratory cultural prompts (assume the role of a Chinese person) shift tendencies.
numbers: No effect sizes on the abstract page. Per Sun & Wang the tasks had 4-21 items each and two models.
limits: Items were withheld, so re-testing needs rebuilt stimuli. Full text not read. The persona result is labelled exploratory by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: original data and items still not seen, so no head-to-head check against Sun & Wang is possible here.

source: Khan, Casper & Hadfield-Menell (2025) Randomness, Not Representation: The Unreliability of Evaluating Cultural Alignment in LLMs. arXiv 2503.08688
finding: Cultural alignment of LLMs is not stable, not extrapolable and not steerable. Trivial format changes often move answers by more than real between-country human variation. Prompt steering to a country gives erratic answers that fail to cluster with the human data.
numbers: One human between-country SD is 0.114; format shifts (direction, identifier vs text) often exceed it. Steerability: LLM-to-human distance divided by human-to-human distance was 6.14 (AlKhamissi prompt) and 1.94 (DSPy-optimised prompt); permutation p=0.0. 15 countries, 180 GQA questions. Extrapolation from few cultural dimensions near chance; with many dimensions ARI above .8 for both LLMs and humans. 813 cover letters, 65 countries, five LLMs.
limits: Models are 2024-early 2025 era. Hiring-letter scenario is an artificial implicit test.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 6: answers to cultural scales swing with wording. A persona label is not a stable individual.

source: Khan et al. (2025) arXiv 2503.08688, case study of Mazeika et al. finding
finding: A published high-level LLM preference finding did not replicate when an indifference option was offered; even vs odd Likert scales gave different country preference patterns.
numbers: 4-point forced choice gave non-uniform country preferences; odd-point scales differed (figures only).
agent_relevance: Any measurement of LLM cultural style needs a neutral option and format controls, or it measures the instrument.

source: Zhang, Xu & Zhang (2026) Aligned but Flattened: Trade-off between Cultural Alignment and Diversity in LLMs. arXiv 2609.00565
finding: Six instruction models prompted with demographic personas on the World Values Survey. Cultural fine-tuning raises alignment but collapses response diversity across personas.
numbers: Diversity: human reference 37.9; vanilla models all above 17.5; every fine-tuned model below 11.0; Gemma-2 gained 2.2 alignment but lost 17 diversity points (to 0.5). Nigerian low-status persona: Qwen alignment fell 51.52 to 37.59 (-27.04%) after fine-tuning. Added subspace under 50% of original dimensions, 25% in Qwen-2.5.
limits: Compares vanilla instruct models with culturally fine-tuned ones, not base vs RLHF. Six 7-8B models only.
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 8 only indirectly: post-training toward group averages squeezes within-group variation, which fits the group-not-individual warning.

source: Hu et al. (2026) Machine Culture. arXiv 2601.17096, Service Persona Camouflage section
finding: The paper names Service Persona Camouflage and blames RLHF, but it did not compare base and tuned models. It is an interpretation, not a tested cause.
numbers: Ideal Affect task: Chinese model with English prompts gave Ideal LAP mean 5.00, SD 0.00, 100% ceiling rate.
limits: Cites prior work for the RLHF argument; text search for base, pretrain, tuned found no ablation.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: the RLHF cause is untested for cultural cognition.

source: Taday Morocho, Cima, Fagni, Avvenuti & Cresci (2026) Assessing the Reliability of Persona-Conditioned LLMs as Synthetic Survey Respondents. WWW Companion 26, arXiv 2602.18462
finding: Demographic persona prompts did not reliably improve match to real US World Values Survey respondents; most items barely changed and a few items and subgroups were distorted.
numbers: Over 70K respondent-item instances; about 2,345-2,359 users per model. Hard similarity: random .273; Llama-2-13B vanilla .370 vs persona .366; Qwen3-4B vanilla .391 vs persona .398. Soft similarity: random .537; Llama-2-13B .621 vs .612; Qwen3-4B .627 vs .627.
limits: Two small open models. US only. One prompt per respondent.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 5, negative: demographic persona alone does not beat no persona at the person level.

source: Venkit, Li, Pruksachatkun & Wu (2026) The Need for a Socially-Grounded Persona Framework for User Simulation (SCOPE). arXiv 2601.07110
finding: Demographic-only personas predict individual human responses poorly; adding traits and identity from a two-hour protocol helps and lowers over-accentuation of demographic differences.
numbers: 141-item protocol, 124 US participants, seven models, 134 evaluation questions. Demographics explain 1.5% of variance in human response similarity. Human baseline within race: White r=.155, Black r=.208 between demographic similarity and response similarity. Generalises to SimBench (441 questions).
limits: US sample of 124. Facets include Big Five, not cultural cognition tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly closed: richer individual data beats group labels, matching Park et al. (0.83 vs 0.74). Equal context length not controlled.

source: Zheng, Pei, Logeswaran, Lee & Jurgens (2024) When 'A Helpful Assistant' Is Not Really Helpful: Personas in System Prompts Do Not Improve Performances of LLMs. arXiv 2311.10054
finding: Adding persona roles to system prompts does not improve accuracy on factual questions versus no persona; best persona per question can help but cannot be picked in advance.
numbers: 162 roles (6 interpersonal types, 8 expertise domains), 4 model families, 2,410 factual questions. Automatic persona choice no better than random.
limits: Roles were not cultural personas; factual questions, not reasoning. Older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: nearest direct test shows persona effects on accuracy are largely random. No cultural-style persona on real reasoning at equal tokens was found.

source: Vignoles et al. (2016) Beyond the East-West dichotomy: global variation in cultural models of selfhood. JEP:General 145(8):966-1000
finding: Seven-dimension model of self-construal (Difference, Connection, Self-Direction, Self-Reliance, Consistency, Self-Expression, Self-Interest) in 16 nations (students) then 55 cultural groups in 33 nations (adults).
numbers: Study 1 N=2,924; Study 2 N=7,279. Individual-level strength of links not obtained.
limits: Only search summaries seen; full text behind a captcha. Cannot say if person-level links are stronger.

source: Search summaries on Lost in Cultural Translation (arXiv 2503.18018) and Mathematics Isn't Culture-Free (arXiv 2507.00883)
finding: Culturally adapted GSM8K problem text lowers accuracy a little; stronger models are more robust.
numbers: 14 models; accuracy drops from 0.3% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to 5.9% (LLaMA 3.1-8B), per a search summary.
limits: Snippet only. Changes item content, not a persona instruction.
agent_relevance: Cultural framing of content costs some accuracy on weak models; not a persona test.

source: Kitayama and colleagues (cited in Na et al. 2010, ref 22); Taras et al. (2013) as summarised in a search result
finding: Small independent studies and reviews report near-zero, negative or mixed correlations among individualism-collectivism scales within samples.
limits: Search snippet; Taras review not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports within-group weakness of scale scores, but is not a clean replication of Na et al.

source: Gap search for an independent replication of Na et al. (2010), incl. the 2023 independent-manifests validation
finding: No independent replication with its own N and per-pair correlations was found this session. arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited (HTTP 429) and web searches were capped.
limits: Absence of search hits is not evidence of absence.

source: Park et al. (2024) Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People, arXiv 2411.10109 (opened in earlier evidence, carried over for gap 5)
finding: Interview-based agents beat demographic agents; not re-opened in this step.
numbers: Interview 0.83 normalized GSS accuracy vs demographic 0.74, persona 0.71.
limits: Interview transcript is far longer than a demographic line, so equal context length is not met.
agent_relevance: The only strong individual-level gain comes from a person's own long data, not a group label.
